info.bio:
Thomas Alan Waits (nacido en Pomona (California) el 7 de diciembre de 1949) es un pianista, cantante, compositor y actor estadounidense, famoso por sus canciones de tono áspero inspiradas en escritores de la generación Beat, en especial Jack Kerouac

En 1967 comenzó a trabajar en los cabarets de Los Ángeles, ambiente que le influyó mucho para las canciones de su primer disco, Closing Time (1973), aunque este álbum se vio eclipsado por The Eagles y Tim Buckley

scenes.name: Cantautores de los setenta
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: James Taylor se convierte, misteriosamente, en el prototipo del cantautor de los setenta; Carole King, Carly Simon y Don McLean, sobrevalorados. Las innovaciones llegan del oeste: Randy Newman y sus viñetas urbanas con fusión de estilos populares, Shawn Phillips, J.J. Cale y su estilo «laid-back», Gram Parsons, Emmylou Harris, Roger McGuinn, Jackson Browne (Late For The Sky) y, sobre todo, Tom Waits, discípulo de Beefheart y cronista de marginados (Swordfishtrombones, Rain Dogs). Excéntricos como Todd Rundgren y Annette Peacock; en Gran Bretaña, Peter Hammill, Anthony Moore, Richard Thompson, Robert Calvert, John Cale, Kevin Coyne, Elton John y los ex Beatles. El realismo de Bruce Springsteen, verdadero heredero de Woody Guthrie y del blues, y la escuela italiana de cantautores (De André, Guccini, Battisti, Sorrenti).

podcast.body: Tom Waits declined an invitation to contribute to the Gorillaz album "Plastic Beach," stating he had "better things to do." "Then again, Johnny Liden and Tom Weitz also said they had better things to do."

podcast.title: Dislike for The Eagles' Cover of "Old 55"
podcast.body: Tom Waits, the original writer of "Old 55," was not a fan of The Eagles' 1974 cover version of his song, finding their recording "too clean" compared to his own interpretation, which he introduced as being about his first real luxury automobile, a 1955 Buick Roadmaster. "Tom Wates thought it was too clean."

podcast.title: Early Career and Discovery
podcast.body: Before his breakthrough, Tom Waits worked as a doorman at a nightclub in San Diego that featured "idiosyncratic performers." He drew the attention of Asylum Records due to his early folk and jazzy style, reminiscent of Joni Mitchell. The label's founders, David Geffen and Elliot Roberts, who were fans of Bob Dylan, saw Waits as a potential "Dylan" for their roster. "Tom caught the attention of Asylum because like the other artists on the label, he was sort of foky at the beginning."

podcast.title: Early Career and Move to LA
podcast.body: Tom Waits got deeply involved with the folk scene in the 1960s, leading him to drop out of high school in his senior year. He then migrated north from suburban San Diego to Los Angeles to pursue his musical ambitions. "Tom Wates was one of those musicians that got involved with the folk scene in the 60s so much so that he dropped out of high school in his senior year and he migrated north from suburban San Diego to LA."

podcast.title: Early Career as Doorman and Asylum Signing
podcast.body: Before gaining attention from Asylum Records, Tom Waits worked as a doorman at a nightclub in San Diego known for featuring idiosyncratic performers. He caught the attention of Asylum because his early work had folk and jazzy elements, similar to other artists on the label like Joni Mitchell. David Geffen and Elliot Roberts, fans of Bob Dylan, saw Waits as potentially their own "Dylan" and were open to experimenting with him, especially given the popularity of the California singer-songwriter scene in the 1970s. "He'd been working as a door man at a nightclub in San Diego that liked to feature some, well, idiosyncratic performers of the day."

podcast.title: Live Performance with Roy Orbison
podcast.body: Tom Waits participated in Roy Orbison's live TV special "A Black and White Night," performing as a backing singer and musician out of admiration for him. "He got inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame and recorded a live TV special, a black and white night, where he was joined by Elvis's 70s backing band, Bruce Springsteen, Elvis Costello, K.D. Lang, Bunny Raite, Jackson Brown and Tom Wait, among others, while just acting as backing singers and musicians for a man they admired."

podcast.title: Musical Style and Categorization
podcast.body: Described as difficult to categorize, Tom Waits was seen as a misfit, a "refugee from the beat era of the 50s" but writing about the 70s. His phrasing, a hybrid spoken/sung scat, owed a strong debt to jazz and blues, with musical accompaniment blending influences from Thelonious Monk, Oscar Brown Jr., and Oscar Peterson. He developed a unique brand of gravelly storytelling. "Wates is a misfit, a refugee from the beat era of the 50s but living and writing very much about the 70s."

podcast.body: Tom Waits and Ricky Lee Jones began a "turbulent relationship" after meeting at The Troubadour. They, along with Chuck Weiss, frequently hung out together, often drinking and doing drugs. "While the three of them did hang out together, usually drinking and doing drugs, she began a bit of a turbulent relationship, not with Chuck E, but with Tom Waits."

podcast.title: Signing with Asylum Records
podcast.body: After being seen performing at The Troubadour in 1971 by Herb Cohen, Waits was signed by Cohen as his manager. Following continued performances, he secured a recording contract with Asylum Records in 1973. "This unique brand of gravelly storytelling led to him getting a manager, Herb Cohen, who saw him at the Trubidor in 1971 and then after he continued to play there, he was signed to a recording contract with Asylum Records in 1973."

podcast.title: The Troubadour Hootnanny Experience
podcast.body: On Mondays, The Troubadour hosted an open mic night called "The Hoot." Tom Waits would arrive when the club opened, around 9 AM, to get his name on the list for a chance to perform a three or four-song set, often waiting all day for his 15 minutes on stage. His first performance there left him "scared shitless." "I used to take the bus to the troubadour and stand out front at 9 o'clock in the morning on a Monday and wait all day to get up and do 15 minutes on stage because you know you never had confidence."

podcast.title: Vocal Evolution and Legendary Self-Harm
podcast.body: Tom Waits's vocal stylings underwent a significant transformation over the years. Initially gruff and soulful, he is said to have deliberately damaged his vocal chords with excessive whiskey and cigarettes, a legendary act intended to cultivate an older, more world-weary sound. This unique approach to his voice often leads to him being listed among singers who are perceived as "unable to sing." "according to legend, he deliberately tortured his vocal chords with lots of whiskey and cigarettes to make him sound older and more world-weary."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
